title: Scalable and Interpretable Representation Alignment with Ordinal Similarity
claim: Alignment between two representation spaces can be measured by checking whether ordinal distance comparisons agree across the spaces.
layout: Top: two formula panels; bottom: visual vs textual panels joined by TSI/QSI connectors
description: The figure has two halves. The top half has two side-by-side titles, 'Triplet Similarity Index' and 'Quadruplet Similarity Index'. Under each is a two-line formula. The first line is sign(d_Vis(pair) − d_Vis(pair)), with circular animal photos (cats and dogs) in place of the variables. The second line is the matching d_Text expression, with words such as 'orange cat' and 'brown dog'. The bottom half has two grey rounded panels, 'Visual Representation' on the left and 'Textual Representation' on the right. The left panel shows four animal photos joined by double-headed arrows. The right panel shows the matching words, with green text and a check mark for the consistent case and red text and a cross for the inconsistent case. V-shaped lines labelled TSI and QSI link the two panels, and a 'Consistent?' label with a check and a cross sits between them. The eye goes first to the titles, then to the photos.
caption: TSI and QSI measure alignment between two representation spaces (e.g., Visual and Textual) by quantifying the consistency of ordinal relationships. TSI checks if relative similarity from an anchor is preserved (e.g., ’Is A closer to B than to C?’). QSI compares relative similarity between distinct pairs (e.g., ’Is A closer to B than C is to D?’)
abstract: Evaluating representation similarity is fundamental to representation learning. However, existing metrics suffer from significant limitations: they lack interpretability due to shifting baselines, lack robustness to outliers, and are computationally intractable for large datasets, forcing reliance on heuristic approximations. To address this, we develop an ordinal-similarity framework, instantiated by the Triplet (TSI) and Quadruplet (QSI) Similarity Indices, which measure alignment by quantifying the consistency of ordinal relationships. We theoretically demonstrate this formulation is inherently interpretable, robust to outliers, and computationally efficient. Finally, we establish a formal equivalence between TSI and local neighborhood alignment, measured by Mutual Nearest Neighbors. Empirically, we validate these properties and show that ordinal similarity offers a scalable approach to measuring alignment, enabling practitioners to better understand and design representations.
